newsitem.title: USA: AT&T finds Pennsylvania costly to enter local service.
newsitem.headline: AT&T finds Pennsylvania costly to enter local service.

text.p: AT&T Corp. may soon find that its efforts to become a local phone service provider along the East Coast stop at Pennsylvania's border.

The long-distance giant, MCI Communications, Sprint Corp. and other competitors are scurrying to become local service providers across the country, after the 1996 Telecommunications Act mandated opening the market.
But AT&T, which dominates Pennsylvania's long distance phone market, is finding it more costly than anticipated to take the local market in the Keystone state, company officials said.
"Pennsylvania is definitely the extreme," said Jim Ginty, AT&T's vice president of government affairs.

The state's Public Utilities Commission is due to release a ruling on July 10 that will set the monthly rates AT&T and its competitors will pay Bell companies for parts of their network to provide local service.

AT&T says those rates could be the highest in the country, based on interim rates the PUC set months ago. They are about twice as high as final rates that already exist in neighboring New Jersey and Delaware, where AT&T will begin providing local service within several months.
The company said the monthly rate in New Jersey is $8.79, while the average rate in Pennsylvania would be $16.98.

"If the rates are so high, we're not going to have an environment in which we can compete successfully with Bell Atlantic," Ginty said. "There's only so much capital a company can spend. (If the rates are high) we'll have to relook at where we'll spend that money."
Bell Atlantic Corp. is Pennsylvania's largest local carrier, serving 4.3 million customers.

So far, 15 long-distance companies have been approved by the PUC to provide local service in Pennsylvania. But Ginty said high rates to purchase local networks could dissuade AT&T and possibly other companies from entering the market.
Despite the good intentions of the Telecommunications Act, some industry analysts say it will take time for meaningful competition to enter the local or long-distance markets.

"Anyone who thought competition would happen 12 months after the act was signed was probably being naive," said Scott Wright at Argus Research. "There's a real friction between local and long-distance companies. I don't think we'll see meaningful competition before the end of 1998."
AT&T said there may be a tendency in some states such as Pennsylvania to protect monopolies, rather than introduce competition.
"There's a tendency to protect existing companies like Bell Atlantic that have a monopoly," Ginty said. "But you can't protect a monopoly and encourage competition at the same time."
Officials at the PUC were not available to comment.

Bell Atlantic officials said they would welcome local competition to their local markets as long as Bell Atlantic can enter the long-distance market without difficulty. But they said that has not happened.

"We have to meet a checklist of items with the Federal Communications Commission that proves our markets are open before we can get into the long-distance market," said Dan Whelan, president of Bell Atlantic Pennsylvania. "AT&T and others continue to challenge that we've met the criteria."
Whelan also said Pennsylvania's rates to buy local networks are actually lower than many states.

"In New York it's $12.49, in Washington D.C. it's $14.92, and in Pennsylvania it's $11.66," he said. "To say that Pennsylvania's rates are out of line is inaccurate. AT&T would like us to give them the local networks for free."
